core.title: Oncology LLM evaluation: From benchmark performance to clinical readiness.
core.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform increasingly well on medical benchmarks, yet benchmark success does not necessarily establish clinical readiness in oncology. Building on recent critiques of medical LLM evaluation, this Perspective identifies four benchmark-practice mismatches: complete-information benchmarks versus active information gathering, single reference answers versus preference-sensitive decisions, cross-sectional snapshots versus longitudinal disease trajectories, and standalone model performance versus model-in-system readiness. To address these gaps, we propose a four-stage evaluation paradigm progressing from a structured knowledge and reasoning baseline to interactive and dialogue-based evaluation, longitudinal trajectory assessment, and model-in-system evaluation. Grounded in the longitudinal, multimodal, and multidisciplinary nature of oncology care, the framework emphasizes the need to calibrate evaluation to intended use and clinical risk and to sustain assessment through continuous monitoring across the model life cycle. Together, these principles offer an operational and oncology-specific pathway for building progressively stronger evidence of clinical readiness.

core.title: One Frozen Simulator Is Not Enough: Simulator Collapse in Multi-Agent RL
core.abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) for human-AI interaction usually trains the agent against a single large language model (LLM) that simulates the user. We show that agents trained this way can systematically fail to generalize, and we trace the failure to simulator collapse: the simulator LLM is mode-collapsed, and a policy trained against it learns narrow strategies that exploit the simulator's mode behavior; these strategies transfer poorly to unseen simulators and to real users. We formalize the collapse and propose two solutions. Verbalized Sampling, applied at inference time, samples each simulator reply from a verbalized response distribution. Co-Training, applied during training similar to self-play, co-evolves the simulator as the policy, so the policy cannot exploit the mode behavior. A population variant samples the simulator for each rollout from a pool of recent checkpoints. We validate both solutions on three benchmarks: Persuasion for Good, tau^2-bench, and CooperBench. Verbalized Sampling improves held-out success by up to 9% over single-simulator RL, and Co-Training pushes gains further to 14%; the human study shows similar gain on real users. Both solutions also preserve the policy diversity that collapses under single-simulator RL. Overall, our findings on simulator collapse point to diverse simulators as a requirement for RL agents that serve real users. We release SCOPE, an open-source framework for Population Co-Training in multi-agent RL.

core.title: TOUCAN: Synthesizing 1.5M Tool-Agentic Data from Real-World MCP Environments
core.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are rapidly emerging as powerful systems for automating tasks across domains. Yet progress in the open-source community is constrained by the lack of high quality permissively licensed tool-agentic training data. Existing datasets are limited in diversity, realism, and complexity, particularly regarding multi-tool and multi-turn interactions. To address this gap, we introduce Toucan, which contains 1.5 million trajectories synthesized from nearly 500 real-world Model Context Protocols (MCPs). Unlike prior work, Toucan leverages authentic MCP environments to generate diverse, realistic, and challenging tasks with trajectories involving real tool execution. Our pipeline first produces a broad spectrum of tool-use queries using five distinct models, applies model-based quality filtering, and then generates agentic trajectories with three teacher models using two agentic frameworks. Rigorous rule-based and model-based validation ensures high-quality outputs. We also introduce three extensions to further diversify tasks and simulate multi-turn conversations. Models fine-tuned on Toucan outperform larger closed-source counterparts on the BFCL V3 benchmark and establish a new Pareto optimum on MCP-Universe Bench.

core.title: Too Many Cooks Spoil The Broth: Auditing Multi-Agent LLM Councils For Medical Reasoning
core.abstract: Multi-agent debate among large language models (LLMs) is widely assumed to improve reasoning by letting models correct one another. We audit that assumption for English medical question answering (QA). Five open-weight 4 to 8B medical and generalist LLMs answer 8,402 questions across six benchmarks as a council, measured against the same five prompted individually and a single larger Qwen3-VL-32B, text-only. The council beats every member on five of six datasets, but most of that accuracy is in place before debate runs: 67% of verdicts settle at Round 0, and on five of six those are the more accurate questions. Where debate runs, opinion change concentrates on one anchor; on the hardest benchmark 85% of moves toward it happen while it is wrong. There, agreement is worth less than disagreement: questions all five agree on are correct 6.6% of the time against 14.6% otherwise, tracking a shared bias toward the first option. The council also trails the larger model on four of six by up to 16.2 points, at seven times the model calls for 1.6 times the compute. Agreement among models is a measurement that can be biased, not evidence of correctness.

core.title: TokenCliff: Benchmarking Output-Token Budget Sensitivity in Multi-Turn LLM Agents
core.abstract: Output-token budgets are a first-order deployment constraint for large language model (LLM) agents, yet existing benchmarks typically evaluate them under a single fixed or generous budget. We introduce TokenCliff, a benchmark for measuring multi-turn agent performance across episode-level output-token budgets. It contains 660 deterministic tasks spanning four capability-oriented domains—file operations, data transformation, tool use, and planning—plus a compositional multi-step split. We propose two budget-sensitivity metrics: Budget Elasticity, which captures robustness across budget levels, and the Cliff Index, which captures the sharpest adjacent-budget performance drop. Evaluating 10 LLMs at five budget levels from 200 to 8,192 tokens yields 33,000 episodes. Results show that (1) accuracy drops by up to 32 percentage points between adjacent budgets; (2) neither peak performance nor larger model size necessarily implies stronger budget elasticity; and (3) budget sensitivity is substantially greater in the evaluated multi-turn setting than in the single-shot diagnostic. Code and data are available in our public repository: https://github.com/BairuiZhang/TokenCliff

core.title: T-MAP: Red-Teaming LLM Agents with Trajectory-aware Evolutionary Search
core.abstract: While prior red-teaming efforts have focused on eliciting harmful text outputs from large language models (LLMs), such approaches fail to capture agent-specific vulnerabilities that emerge through multi-step tool execution, particularly in rapidly growing ecosystems such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP). To address this gap, we propose a trajectory-aware evolutionary search method, T-MAP, which leverages execution trajectories to guide the discovery of adversarial prompts. Our approach enables the automatic generation of attacks that not only bypass safety guardrails but also reliably realize harmful objectives through actual tool interactions. Empirical evaluations across diverse MCP environments demonstrate that T-MAP substantially outperforms baselines in attack realization rate (ARR) and remains effective against frontier models, including GPT-5.2, Gemini-3-Pro, Qwen3.5, and GLM-5, thereby revealing previously underexplored vulnerabilities in autonomous LLM agents. Code is available at https://github.com/pwnhyo/T-MAP.
